scope: Mobbin section research for Moriz Studio, a web/app design and development studio
method: Twelve focused searches; returned images visually inspected before selection. No live-site interaction or performance testing.

searches.query: Digital agency hero section with a headline explaining design and development services and featured client work
Agency services section showing website design, software development and digital product capabilities
Design agency portfolio section showing selected client projects with large images and project descriptions
Agency homepage opening section with a large positioning headline and a short explanation of the digital products the studio builds
Agency project case study section explaining the client challenge, design solution and final digital product
Agency process section describing how a client starts a project from discovery through design and development
Agency testimonial section with a client quote and the client's name, role and organization
Agency contact section inviting prospective clients to discuss a project
Agency frequently asked questions section answering questions about working together
basement.studio featured projects section with project images, descriptions and service labels
Büro frequently asked questions about client projects and working with the agency
Büro client testimonial quote with the speaker's name, company and role

selected.title: Large positioning statement with client proof
selected.observation: A large studio statement sits above a short explanation and a multi-row client-logo grid.
selected.benefit: The agency’s category and supporting proof are visible together.
selected.tradeoff: The dense logo wall takes substantial space; it does not explain each engagement or contribution.
selected.application: Use the relationship between claim and evidence. Moriz already has a logo strip; add only accurately attributed organizations and retain the agreed hero copy.

selected.title: Service promise paired with real work
selected.observation: A short service statement and explanatory paragraph sit beside a large Notion campaign image, with an offerings link.
selected.benefit: A capability claim is paired with an example rather than an abstract icon.
selected.tradeoff: This image demonstrates brand work; it does not establish software delivery or technical depth.
selected.application: When relevant assets are available, connect each confirmed theme to real work. Keep the current three themes; do not introduce extra service categories.

selected.title: Services grouped into two domains
selected.observation: A red section splits a portrait, category labels, and service lists into columns. Digital and Branding are separate groups.
selected.benefit: Visitors can distinguish service families and scan the individual disciplines.
selected.tradeoff: The list is long, and its scope includes many capabilities not established for Moriz.
selected.application: Use grouping to clarify specification, UX/UI and development coverage. Include only confirmed capabilities; do not copy the agency’s service list.

selected.title: Technical capabilities made explicit
selected.observation: Three compact capability columns include design, engineering and commerce terms. A project-start button sits at the lower right.
selected.benefit: Engineering work is named explicitly alongside design.
selected.tradeoff: Dense technical terminology and commerce-specific scope may be difficult for small-business buyers.
selected.application: Consider a short, plain-language explanation of design and development coverage when content is reviewed. The visible extra contact button is not a fit for the confirmed floating-only WhatsApp choice.

selected.title: Editorial project grid with context
selected.observation: An uneven two-column grid combines project imagery, names, short descriptions and small classification labels.
selected.benefit: The description gives each visual a purpose; individual projects retain their own character.
selected.tradeoff: Staggered reading order needs care on mobile and in RTL. It is an alternative composition, not evidence to replace the approved rows.
selected.application: Carry project name, what was built and Moriz’s contribution alongside each image within the existing project-row layout.

selected.title: Product previews with visible project titles
selected.observation: A selected-work heading precedes a two-column collection of large previews. Project names and small labels appear over the tiles; one tile has a case-study label.
selected.benefit: Digital artifacts occupy most of the space and make product output visible.
selected.tradeoff: Several previews are darkened in this capture, and overlaid text depends on contrast. Their hover and link behavior cannot be verified.
selected.application: Prefer real product screenshots or recordings over generic mockups when assets arrive. Retain visible names and a clear link to each existing project page.

selected.title: Narrative topics beside large project media
selected.observation: A narrow left column shows the Lyft project identity, a visible challenge paragraph and topic labels; large project visuals fill the right column.
selected.benefit: The visual work is accompanied by a narrative entry point and a list of project topics.
selected.tradeoff: Only the challenge text is expanded in the screenshot. Sticky navigation, other topic content and mobile behavior are unverified.
selected.application: Use problem, audience, contribution, solution and verified outcomes as questions to investigate in future case studies. Keep the existing four details per project until their questions and answers are agreed.

selected.title: Customer evidence with concrete outcome fields
selected.observation: A customer-story panel pairs imagery with a business-use headline, a quote, three outcome fields and attributed speaker details.
selected.benefit: It demonstrates how a product story can connect an artifact to practical use and reported outcomes.
selected.tradeoff: This is a software customer story, not an agency portfolio. Its figures are that customer’s claims and cannot establish Moriz’s results.
selected.application: Use actual usage or outcome evidence only when its source, timeframe and Moriz’s role are supplied. Do not fill missing data with decorative metrics.

selected.title: Numbered stages with explanatory copy
selected.observation: Four vertically stacked numbered stages pair large titles with short explanatory paragraphs.
selected.benefit: The stages are readable in a still image and do not rely on a hidden interaction to communicate their meaning.
selected.tradeoff: This describes a full branding engagement, rather than just starting a client relationship.
selected.application: Apply the clear numbering to the already confirmed starting steps: initial 5–10 minute call, in-depth specification discussion, then a quote. Supporting copy remains to be agreed.

selected.title: Approach connected to creative technology
selected.observation: A large approach statement sits above a two-by-two set of short descriptions for strategy, direction, design and creative technology.
selected.benefit: Technology is presented as part of a broader delivery approach.
selected.tradeoff: The oversized paragraph is demanding to scan, and these four stages are not Moriz’s confirmed client-starting steps.
selected.application: Useful as a comparison for explaining the connection between research, design and implementation in future About or case-study content. Keep the homepage starting section focused on how the client begins.

selected.title: Quote with separate speaker attribution
selected.observation: A large client quote occupies the right side; the speaker, organization and role sit in a smaller left column.
selected.benefit: The source of the endorsement is visible beside the statement.
selected.tradeoff: A long quote uses substantial page height. The still image does not establish a carousel or its controls.
selected.application: Select from the five reported testimonials and preserve accurate attribution. A quote related to the featured project may offer more context; this is a research hypothesis.

selected.title: Questions about working with the agency
selected.observation: Seven numbered FAQ rows address client fit, scope, industries, capacity and technology. The first answer is visible; the other rows show collapsed states.
selected.benefit: The topics concern decisions a prospective client may need to make before starting.
selected.tradeoff: The expanded body appears low contrast in the capture. Interaction semantics and keyboard behavior are untested.
selected.application: Use real client questions when the owner supplies them. Keep the confirmed FAQ position. Client fit and phase-specific engagements are candidate research topics, not approved questions or answers.

selected.title: Practical objections collected in one place
selected.observation: A large FAQ introduction precedes six rows covering output, starting requirements, brand fit, ownership, turnaround and team relationships. One answer is visible.
selected.benefit: The questions are concrete and focus on practical purchase concerns.
selected.tradeoff: AI asset production differs from web-system work; its scope and promises cannot transfer directly.
selected.application: Compare topic coverage with actual Moriz inquiries. Inputs, ownership and handover may merit investigation; publish answers only after the owner confirms the facts.

selected.title: A concentrated closing invitation
selected.observation: A dark contact section contains a small invitation label and a large multi-line message about a new project or collaboration.
selected.benefit: Contact intent is immediately legible through scale and concentration.
selected.tradeoff: No functional contact action is visible in this crop, so a complete inquiry flow cannot be inferred.
selected.application: Use the section’s focus as a content comparison. Contact content remains open, and the floating WhatsApp control remains the confirmed inquiry access.
